screens.title: Advanced Ansible: Roles, Variables, and Templates
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn three interlocking capabilities that make Ansible ready for production: roles to structure automation, variables to parameterize behavior, and Jinja2 templates to produce host-specific configuration files. You will see why roles transform a sprawling playbook into a modular, reusable package that groups tasks, handlers, templates, and variable files. You will learn how variable scopes and precedence let you override settings safely per environment, and how to keep secrets out of plain text by choosing the right storage mechanism. You will also learn how the template module renders Jinja2 templates and how handlers, triggered by notify, ensure services restart only when needed. Throughout, concrete examples use an Nginx role with a template for the default site and a handler that restarts the service only when configuration truly changed. By the end, you will be able to refactor a flat playbook into a role, change a port using a variable, and deploy a rendered configuration without causing unnecessary restarts. Consider how modularity and idempotency change the way you maintain infrastructure: what manual steps will you remove first?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Overview
Advanced Ansible: Roles, Variables, and Templates
Organize automation, parameterize behavior, and render dynamic files safely at scale.
What you'll understand

How roles structure related content, how variables make playbooks reusable across environments, how Jinja2 templates generate per-host configs, and how handlers prevent unnecessary restarts.

Instructor Note
This chapter focuses on practical refactoring: move tasks into a role, define variables, render templates, and wire a handler to restart only on change.
Explore Key Topics
Roles
Standardized directories that group tasks, handlers, templates, and vars into reusable units.
Variables
Parameterize playbooks; placed in defaults, vars, inventory, or playbooks with a clear precedence order.
Templates
Jinja2 templates render host-specific configuration files, using the template module to copy rendered output.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Nginx Role (visual)
A role bundles tasks, templates, vars, defaults, and handlers so your main playbook stays concise.
tasks/main.yml
Installs Nginx, copies index.html, renders template, notifies restart.
templates/default.conf.j2
Server block using {{ nginx_port }} and {{ nginx_root_dir }} placeholders.
Tip: start by moving installation tasks into roles, then add variables and templates to parameterize environments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will be able to organize a playbook into roles, define and scope variables, use Jinja2 templates to render configuration files, and wire handlers so services restart only when necessary. First, you will learn the anatomy of a role and why roles make automation reusable across projects. Second, you will practice defining variables in defaults, vars, and inventory and learn where to place values to make overrides predictable. Third, you will write a Jinja2 template that uses variables and an Ansible built-in variable to generate a per-host configuration. Fourth, you will implement handlers and the notify mechanism so a restart runs only when configuration actually changes. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic to help you remember the structure and a verified competency milestone to guide your practice. These skills reduce manual steps, improve safety, and make deployments repeatable in development and production. Which environment will you refactor first using roles?

screens.title: Roles: Definition and Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: A role is a standardized, reusable directory structure in Ansible that groups related tasks, handlers, templates, and variables into a single unit. Roles replace sprawling inline tasks by collocating everything needed to configure a component, such as Nginx, inside roles/nginx. This makes a role portable: you can reuse it in other playbooks or projects without copying tasks and files around. Concretely, a role typically contains tasks/main. yml, handlers/main. yml, templates/*. j2, vars/main. yml, and defaults/main. yml. That structure makes intent clear and separates defaults from overrides. For example, move your Nginx installation, template deployment, and service management into roles/nginx/tasks/main. yml and let the main playbook simply reference 'roles: - nginx'. A common misconception is that roles add complexity—roles actually reduce cognitive load once you adopt the pattern because each role has a clear responsibility. When you design roles, prefer one responsibility per role, and avoid putting unrelated tasks together. Now, think of one service in your environment that would benefit from a role and how you would name it. Roles: Definition and Purpose means encapsulate tasks, handlers, templates, and variables into a role so the main playbook stays concise and reusable.. In practical terms, what a role is and why it matters for maintainable automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Roles: Definition
What is a Role?
A role is a directory with a fixed layout that holds tasks, handlers, templates, variables, and defaults for a specific responsibility.
Why use roles
  • Collocates all files for a component for clarity and reuse.
  • Makes playbooks shorter and easier to read.
  • Enables sharing roles across projects or teams.
Common misconception
Some think roles add unnecessary layers. In practice roles reduce duplication and make maintenance safer as projects grow.
Key Takeaway

Adopt one responsibility per role. Roles are the primary unit of reuse and clarity in Ansible projects.

Role directory example
roles/
└── nginx/
    ├── tasks/
    │   └── main.yml
    ├── handlers/
    │   └── main.yml
    ├── templates/
    │   └── nginx.conf.j2
    ├── vars/
    │   └── main.yml
    └── defaults/
        └── main.yml
Concrete example
Refactor a flat playbook so that installing Nginx and deploying site files move into roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml. The main playbook then lists the role name only.

screens.title: Role Directory Structure
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the role layout is critical to using roles effectively. Each folder has a clear purpose. tasks contains the sequence of operations to reach the desired state; handlers contains tasks triggered by notify, usually service restarts; templates holds Jinja2 files rendered with variables; vars and defaults hold variable files, with defaults intended for low-priority defaults and vars for stronger values; files can hold static files to copy. For example, put nginx_port and nginx_root_dir in defaults when you want sensible defaults that users can override, but put environment-specific values in inventory or higher-precedence vars when necessary. Using this layout avoids scattering config and reduces accidental duplication. A typical mistake is putting secrets in vars files under version control; use Ansible Vault for secrets instead. Finally, naming matters: use descriptive role names like nginx, database, or application to make catalogs discoverable. Which folder will you inspect first when you debug a role? Role Directory Structure means follow the standard role layout so each file type has an obvious home and variable precedence stays predictable.. In practical terms, what each folder in a role contains and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Role Structure
Role folder purpose
tasks/
Sequence of steps to configure the component. This is the role's core logic.
handlers/
Tasks that run when notified, typically to restart or reload services.
templates/
Jinja2 templates rendered per host, used with the template module to create config files.
vars/ and defaults/
defaults/ holds low-priority defaults; vars/ holds higher-priority role variables. Prefer defaults for user-overridable settings.
Practical example
# roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml
nginx_port: 80
nginx_root_dir: /var/www/html

# roles/nginx/vars/main.yml
# Use vars for values you don't expect to override often
Misconception
Putting secrets directly in vars/main.yml is risky. Instead, use Ansible Vault to encrypt sensitive variable files before committing.
Why it matters

A predictable role layout speeds onboarding and debugging, and supports environment-specific overrides without changing role internals.

screens.title: Using a Role in a Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Using a role in a playbook is straightforward: list the role name under roles and let Ansible pull tasks, handlers, templates, and variables from the role directory. This replaces long task lists in the playbook with a single, descriptive line that declares intent. For example, a webserver play that uses the nginx role begins with hosts, become, then a roles section containing 'nginx'. When you run ansible-playbook, Ansible loads the role in the order specified, applies defaults, evaluates variables according to precedence, executes tasks, and collects notifications for handlers. A common mistake is assuming the playbook's variables always override role defaults; variable precedence determines the actual value and can lead to confusion unless you follow naming and placement conventions. After referencing the role, test the playbook: run it in a development inventory, check the rendered configuration, and confirm that the handler only runs when a change occurs. If a role needs configuration, supply variables in inventory or in vars files that intentionally override defaults. Using a Role in a Playbook means call roles by name in the playbook. the role supplies the implementation while the playbook declares what to deploy.. In practical terms, reference roles so the playbook stays concise and declarative. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Playbook = Declaration
keyIdea.text: Call roles by name in the playbook. The role supplies the implementation while the playbook declares what to deploy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Use in Playbook
Minimal playbook using a role
---
- name: Deploy web server with Nginx role
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  roles:
    - nginx
This single declaration leverages the entire role. The playbook states intent: deploy the webserver, while the role contains the implementation details.
Check
Run the playbook against a development inventory and verify the role's templates and tasks executed as expected.
Variable overrides
If the role defines nginx_port in defaults, you can override it in inventory or in the playbook vars so different environments use different ports.
Misconception
Putting all overrides in the playbook reduces flexibility. Prefer inventory or group_vars for environment-specific values.
Try this

Change nginx_port in inventory, re-run the playbook, and confirm the server listens on the new port.

screens.title: Variables: Purpose and Locations
screens.narratorSegment: Variables let you avoid hardcoded values and make the same automation work across development, staging, and production. In a role context, variables can live in defaults for low-priority defaults, in vars for stronger role-level values, in inventory or group_vars for environment-specific settings, or even in the playbook itself for one-off overrides. Choosing where to define a variable affects who can override it later because Ansible follows a defined precedence order. For example, defining nginx_port in roles/nginx/defaults/main. yml gives a sensible default of 80 that any inventory or higher-precedence source can override. A concrete example: set nginx_root_dir in defaults, then override it in inventory for a staging host that uses a different path. A common pitfall is assuming a variable defined in defaults will never be overridden; in practice inventory and host vars will take precedence. Also, avoid committing secrets into plain var files—use Ansible Vault to encrypt sensitive variable files. Which variable would you make an inventory override for your environment? Variables: Purpose and Locations means place common defaults in defaults, stronger role values in vars, and environment-specific values in inventory or group_vars to control overrides.. In practical terms, parameterize playbooks with variables and choose the right place to store them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Place common defaults in defaults, stronger role values in vars, and environment-specific values in inventory or group_vars to control overrides.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Variables
Where to define variables
defaults/
Low-priority defaults intended to be overridden by inventory or play-level vars.
vars/
Role-level variables with higher precedence than defaults. Use sparingly for values you don't expect to override.
inventory / group_vars / host_vars
Environment-specific values. These typically determine what differs between dev, staging, and production.
Example
# roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml
nginx_port: 80
nginx_root_dir: /var/www/html

# inventory.ini (override for staging)
[webservers]
staging1 ansible_host=10.0.0.5 nginx_port=8080
Misconception
Variables in defaults are safe to commit. They are safe, but avoid placing secrets in defaults. For secrets use Ansible Vault.
Why it matters

Correct placement lets teams override configuration without editing role internals, enabling safe reuse across environments.

screens.title: Variable Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible supports variables from many sources and applies a precedence order to determine the final value. Understanding precedence prevents surprises when values come from defaults, role vars, inventory, host_vars, group_vars, or the playbook. The safe rule is: lower-priority defaults are intentionally easy to override, while higher-precedence places like host_vars or play vars take priority. For example, if nginx_port is set to 80 in defaults but the inventory defines nginx_port as 8080 for a host, the inventory value wins. A mistaken assumption is that role vars always override inventory; in reality the precise precedence list matters. When debugging unexpected values, inspect each possible source starting from the playbook and inventory down to role defaults. Also consider that extra mechanisms like extra-vars passed on the command line have the highest precedence. Always document where your team expects to set environment-specific values to avoid conflicting overrides. Variable Precedence means when multiple definitions exist, ansible uses a strict precedence order — inspect higher-priority sources first when debugging.. In practical terms, how ansible decides which variable value wins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Precedence Determines Effective Value
keyIdea.text: When multiple definitions exist, Ansible uses a strict precedence order — inspect higher-priority sources first when debugging.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Variable Precedence
Quick precedence guide
  1. Extra vars (highest)
  2. Play vars
  3. Host vars / inventory
  4. Role vars
  5. defaults/main.yml (lowest)
Example
If defaults set nginx_port to 80, and inventory sets it to 8080, the inventory value applies.
Debugging tip
Use ansible-playbook with increased verbosity to see which variable values are applied, and check group_vars, host_vars, and extra-vars when values conflict.
Common mistake
Assuming defaults are immutable. Defaults are intentionally overrideable; place environment-specific values higher in precedence.
Key Takeaway

Place values where the intended override behavior is clear, and document conventions for your team.

screens.title: Using Variables Inside Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Variables become useful when referenced inside tasks. In a task that ensures Nginx listens on the configured port, you can use a template or lineinfile task that refers to nginx_port. For example, a lineinfile task can search for a listen directive and replace it with a line containing the variable. When that task changes the file, it should notify a handler named restart nginx. The notify ensures the service restarts only when the content actually changed, preserving idempotency. A concrete example from the chapter uses lineinfile with a regexp to ensure the listen line matches 'listen {{ nginx_port }};'. After a change, the handler defined in roles/nginx/handlers/main. yml runs the service restart. A common mistake is forgetting notify on tasks that alter configuration, which results in changes not applying until a manual restart. As you write tasks, always consider whether a change requires a handler and test both the modified file and service status after running the playbook. Using Variables Inside Tasks means reference variables inside tasks and use notify so handlers run only when tasks actually make changes.. In practical terms, referencing variables in tasks and notifying handlers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Variables in Tasks
Task example
- name: Ensure Nginx listens on specified port
  ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
    regexp: 'listen {{ nginx_port }};'
    line: '    listen {{ nginx_port }};'
    state: present
  notify: restart nginx
This task uses the nginx_port variable and notifies a handler when it changes the file. The handler then restarts the service once per play if needed.
Handler example
- name: restart nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
Common mistake
Forgetting to add notify means the service will not restart automatically after config changes, which can leave servers running stale configurations.

Always pair tasks that change configuration with notify to trigger handlers and keep services in sync.

screens.title: Jinja2 Templating Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Jinja2 templating lets you embed variables and simple logic inside configuration files so Ansible can render per-host configurations. Templates use double curly braces to reference variables, for example 'listen {{ nginx_port }};' or 'root {{ nginx_root_dir }};'. Templates can also reference Ansible built-in variables such as inventory_hostname to include the host's identity inside the file. The template lives under roles/nginx/templates and is processed by the ansible. builtin. template module on the control node before being copied to the managed host. An important practical tip is to keep template logic simple: use variables and minimal conditionals to avoid complexity. A common misconception is that templates execute arbitrary code on hosts; templates are rendered locally and produce plain text files that are then transferred. When testing, change a variable such as nginx_port from 80 to 8080, re-run the playbook, and inspect the rendered file on the host to confirm the substitution happened as expected. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Jinja2 Templates
Template example
server {
    listen {{ nginx_port }};
    server_name {{ inventory_hostname }};

    root {{ nginx_root_dir }};
    index index.html index.htm;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }
}
This template uses variables for port and root and a built-in variable for server name, producing a host-specific server block.
Rendering with template module
When Ansible runs the template module, it replaces placeholders with variable values and copies the rendered file to the destination on the managed host.
Misconception
Templates do not execute code on the managed host. Rendering happens on the control node and produces a plain text file transferred to the host.
Key Takeaway

Keep template logic minimal and test rendered output to ensure variables substitute as expected.

screens.title: Template Module and Rendering Flow
screens.narratorSegment: The template module orchestrates three steps: render, check, and copy. First, Ansible renders the Jinja2 template locally on the control node using the available variables. Second, Ansible compares the rendered content to the existing file on the managed host; if they differ, a change is registered. Third, if changed, Ansible copies the new file to the destination with specified ownership and permissions. This check-before-copy behavior is important because it connects to handlers: if the template task reports a change, it can notify a handler like restart nginx, and the handler will run at the end of the play. This prevents unnecessary restarts when content is identical. A practical example is updating nginx_port in defaults, rendering default. conf. j2, and seeing a notified restart only when content actually changed. A common error is assuming template always forces change; in fact it is idempotent because Ansible compares before applying. When testing, inspect the playbook output to see whether the template task changed the file and whether the handler ran. Template Module and Rendering Flow means template renders locally, ansible checks for differences, and copies only when necessary; changes can notify handlers for conditional actions.. In practical terms, how the template module processes jinja2 templates and deploys the result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Template Module Flow
Template module steps
1. Render
Jinja2 template is rendered locally using variables.
2. Compare
Ansible checks whether the rendered file differs from the remote file.
3. Copy
If different, the file is copied and change is reported, potentially notifying handlers.
Because Ansible compares before copying, templates are idempotent and only cause changes when content truly differs. This behavior is what lets notify and handlers prevent unnecessary restarts.
Practical check
Change nginx_port in defaults to 8080, run the playbook, and watch whether the template task reports a change and whether the handler restarts the service once.
Key Takeaway

Template module renders then applies only if needed, enabling efficient, idempotent configuration management.

screens.title: Handlers and notify
screens.narratorSegment: Handlers are special tasks that run only when notified by another task and they run at the end of the play. Typical uses include restarting or reloading services after a configuration change. A task that modifies a configuration file should include notify with the handler's name so the handler executes only if the task made a change. For example, a template task that updates /etc/nginx/sites-available/default can include notify: restart nginx. If multiple tasks notify the same handler, the handler still runs only once at the end of the play, which prevents repeated restarts. Handlers help preserve idempotency and reduce disruptive operations. A common misconception is that handlers run immediately; they do not—they queue and run at the end. When designing handlers, keep them simple and idempotent themselves, and test that the handler runs only when the intended change occurs by examining the play output and service status after running the playbook. Handlers and notify means use notify in changing tasks and define handlers to perform the reaction; handlers run at the end and only once even if notified multiple times.. In practical terms, trigger actions only when changes occur to keep systems efficient. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Handlers
Handler pattern
# task that changes config
- name: Configure Nginx default site
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: default.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
  notify: restart nginx

# roles/nginx/handlers/main.yml
- name: restart nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
Why handlers matter
They prevent unnecessary or repeated service restarts by running once at the end of the play only if a notifying task reported a change.
Misconception
Handlers do not run immediately after notify. They are queued and run at the end, ensuring consolidated actions.
Try this

Make a harmless change in the template, run the playbook, and observe that the handler runs once at the end only when the template changed.

screens.title: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a few pragmatic best practices to make roles reliable and maintainable. First, design each role for a single responsibility: keep database, webserver, and application roles separate. Second, place non-sensitive defaults in defaults/main. yml, but never commit secrets in plain var files—use Ansible Vault to encrypt secrets. Third, prefer inventory or group_vars for environment-specific overrides rather than editing role internals. Fourth, test roles in a development environment and verify idempotency by re-running the playbook; a well-designed role should report no changes on a second run unless input variables changed. Fifth, document variable names and expected types so teammates know how to override settings without guessing. Common pitfalls include misunderstanding variable precedence and forgetting notify on tasks that alter configuration. When debugging, enable verbosity to examine variable values and task outcomes. Finally, make small, incremental changes and verify the rendered template and service state to avoid widespread disruptions. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn three interlocking capabilities that make Ansible ready for production: roles to structure automation, variables to parameterize behavior, and Jinja2 templates to produce host-specific configuration files. You will see why roles transform a sprawling playbook into a modular, reusable package that groups tasks, handlers, templates, and variable files. You will learn how variable scopes and precedence let you override settings safely per environment, and how to keep secrets out of plain text by choosing the right storage mechanism. You will also learn how the template module renders Jinja2 templates and how handlers, triggered by notify, ensure services restart only when needed. Throughout, concrete examples use an Nginx role with a template for the default site and a handler that restarts the service only when configuration truly changed. By the end, you will be able to refactor a flat playbook into a role, change a port using a variable, and deploy a rendered configuration without causing unnecessary restarts. Consider how modularity and idempotency change the way you maintain infrastructure: what manual steps will you remove first?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to organize a playbook into roles, define and scope variables, use Jinja2 templates to render configuration files, and wire handlers so services restart only when necessary. First, you will learn the anatomy of a role and why roles make automation reusable across projects. Second, you will practice defining variables in defaults, vars, and inventory and learn where to place values to make overrides predictable. Third, you will write a Jinja2 template that uses variables and an Ansible built-in variable to generate a per-host configuration. Fourth, you will implement handlers and the notify mechanism so a restart runs only when configuration actually changes. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic to help you remember the structure and a verified competency milestone to guide your practice. These skills reduce manual steps, improve safety, and make deployments repeatable in development and production. Which environment will you refactor first using roles?

This second objectives slide focuses on the skills you will practice. You will learn to create the role directory layout, populate defaults and vars, author a Jinja2 template for Nginx, add a handler to restart the service, and execute the site playbook to verify results. The activity walks through creating the roles/nginx directory, adding tasks that install packages and use the template module, and wiring notify to a restart handler. You will also learn to change a variable, re-run the playbook, and confirm the rendered configuration reflects the new value. Finally, you will practice a short checklist: run in a development environment, confirm idempotency, review variable precedence if values differ, and avoid placing secrets in plain vars files. These hands-on steps prepare you to maintain automation with confidence and reduce manual server edits.

A role is a standardized, reusable directory structure in Ansible that groups related tasks, handlers, templates, and variables into a single unit. Roles replace sprawling inline tasks by collocating everything needed to configure a component, such as Nginx, inside roles/nginx. This makes a role portable: you can reuse it in other playbooks or projects without copying tasks and files around. Concretely, a role typically contains tasks/main. yml, handlers/main. yml, templates/*. j2, vars/main. yml, and defaults/main. yml. That structure makes intent clear and separates defaults from overrides. For example, move your Nginx installation, template deployment, and service management into roles/nginx/tasks/main. yml and let the main playbook simply reference 'roles: - nginx'. A common misconception is that roles add complexity—roles actually reduce cognitive load once you adopt the pattern because each role has a clear responsibility. When you design roles, prefer one responsibility per role, and avoid putting unrelated tasks together. Now, think of one service in your environment that would benefit from a role and how you would name it. Roles: Definition and Purpose means encapsulate tasks, handlers, templates, and variables into a role so the main playbook stays concise and reusable.. In practical terms, what a role is and why it matters for maintainable automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the role layout is critical to using roles effectively. Each folder has a clear purpose. tasks contains the sequence of operations to reach the desired state; handlers contains tasks triggered by notify, usually service restarts; templates holds Jinja2 files rendered with variables; vars and defaults hold variable files, with defaults intended for low-priority defaults and vars for stronger values; files can hold static files to copy. For example, put nginx_port and nginx_root_dir in defaults when you want sensible defaults that users can override, but put environment-specific values in inventory or higher-precedence vars when necessary. Using this layout avoids scattering config and reduces accidental duplication. A typical mistake is putting secrets in vars files under version control; use Ansible Vault for secrets instead. Finally, naming matters: use descriptive role names like nginx, database, or application to make catalogs discoverable. Which folder will you inspect first when you debug a role? Role Directory Structure means follow the standard role layout so each file type has an obvious home and variable precedence stays predictable.. In practical terms, what each folder in a role contains and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Using a role in a playbook is straightforward: list the role name under roles and let Ansible pull tasks, handlers, templates, and variables from the role directory. This replaces long task lists in the playbook with a single, descriptive line that declares intent. For example, a webserver play that uses the nginx role begins with hosts, become, then a roles section containing 'nginx'. When you run ansible-playbook, Ansible loads the role in the order specified, applies defaults, evaluates variables according to precedence, executes tasks, and collects notifications for handlers. A common mistake is assuming the playbook's variables always override role defaults; variable precedence determines the actual value and can lead to confusion unless you follow naming and placement conventions. After referencing the role, test the playbook: run it in a development inventory, check the rendered configuration, and confirm that the handler only runs when a change occurs. If a role needs configuration, supply variables in inventory or in vars files that intentionally override defaults. Using a Role in a Playbook means call roles by name in the playbook. the role supplies the implementation while the playbook declares what to deploy.. In practical terms, reference roles so the playbook stays concise and declarative. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Variables let you avoid hardcoded values and make the same automation work across development, staging, and production. In a role context, variables can live in defaults for low-priority defaults, in vars for stronger role-level values, in inventory or group_vars for environment-specific settings, or even in the playbook itself for one-off overrides. Choosing where to define a variable affects who can override it later because Ansible follows a defined precedence order. For example, defining nginx_port in roles/nginx/defaults/main. yml gives a sensible default of 80 that any inventory or higher-precedence source can override. A concrete example: set nginx_root_dir in defaults, then override it in inventory for a staging host that uses a different path. A common pitfall is assuming a variable defined in defaults will never be overridden; in practice inventory and host vars will take precedence. Also, avoid committing secrets into plain var files—use Ansible Vault to encrypt sensitive variable files. Which variable would you make an inventory override for your environment? Variables: Purpose and Locations means place common defaults in defaults, stronger role values in vars, and environment-specific values in inventory or group_vars to control overrides.. In practical terms, parameterize playbooks with variables and choose the right place to store them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible supports variables from many sources and applies a precedence order to determine the final value. Understanding precedence prevents surprises when values come from defaults, role vars, inventory, host_vars, group_vars, or the playbook. The safe rule is: lower-priority defaults are intentionally easy to override, while higher-precedence places like host_vars or play vars take priority. For example, if nginx_port is set to 80 in defaults but the inventory defines nginx_port as 8080 for a host, the inventory value wins. A mistaken assumption is that role vars always override inventory; in reality the precise precedence list matters. Jinja2 templating lets you embed variables and simple logic inside configuration files so Ansible can render per-host configurations. Templates use double curly braces to reference variables, for example 'listen {{ nginx_port }};' or 'root {{ nginx_root_dir }};'. Templates can also reference Ansible built-in variables such as inventory_hostname to include the host's identity inside the file. The template module orchestrates three steps: render, check, and copy. First, Ansible renders the Jinja2 template locally on the control node using the available variables. Second, Ansible compares the rendered content to the existing file on the managed host; if they differ, a change is registered. Third, if changed, Ansible copies the new file to the destination with specified ownership and permissions. This check-before-copy behavior is important because it connects to handlers: if the template task reports a change, it can notify a handler like restart nginx, and the handler will run at the end of the play. This prevents unnecessary restarts when content is identical. Handlers are special tasks that run only when notified by another task and they run at the end of the play. Typical uses include restarting or reloading services after a configuration change. A task that modifies a configuration file should include notify with the handler's name so the handler executes only if the task made a change. For example, a template task that updates /etc/nginx/sites-available/default can include notify: restart nginx. If multiple tasks notify the same handler, the handler still runs only once at the end of the play, which prevents repeated restarts. Handlers help preserve idempotency and reduce disruptive operations. A common misconception is that handlers run immediately; they do not—they queue and run at the end. Follow a few pragmatic best practices to make roles reliable and maintainable. First, design each role for a single responsibility: keep database, webserver, and application roles separate. Second, place non-sensitive defaults in defaults/main. yml, but never commit secrets in plain var files—use Ansible Vault to encrypt secrets. Third, prefer inventory or group_vars for environment-specific overrides rather than editing role internals. Fourth, test roles in a development environment and verify idempotency by re-running the playbook; a well-designed role should report no changes on a second run unless input variables changed. Fifth, document variable names and expected types so teammates know how to override settings without guessing. Finally, make small, incremental changes and verify the rendered template and service state to avoid widespread disruptions. Here are three core concepts to remember. First, a role is a standardized directory layout that groups tasks, handlers, templates, and variables so automation becomes modular and reusable. Second, variables parameterize playbooks; place defaults in defaults/main. yml and use inventory or host_vars for environment-specific overrides, keeping secrets out of plain text. Third, Jinja2 templates are text files with placeholders that Ansible renders and copies to a managed host; they let you create host-specific configuration files using both custom variables and Ansible built-in variables like inventory_hostname.
